articles.title: New York Giants' Francis Mauigoa ready to face the man he once idolized
articles.summary: New York Giants rookie OL Francis Mauigoa once idolized Aaron Donald, and now he'll face him on Monday night.
articles.body:
Los Angeles Rams legendary defensive tackle and future Hall of Famer Aaron Donald returns to the field on Monday night against the New York Giants after two years away.

Waiting for him will be Giants rookie guard Francis "Sisi" Mauigoa, the 10th overall selection in this year's NFL draft, who, like many young players, idolized Donald growing up.

Donald, 35, retired after the 2023 season and is said to be in game shape. He will have to be. Mauigoa is one of the league's promising new stars. This game will be a battle for everyone to focus on.

Mauigoa, who stands 6-foot-6, weighs 330 pounds, and plays with a chip on his shoulder, is ready.

"It's going to be a tough challenge," Mauigoa told NJ Advance Media this week . "The best opponent I'll ever go against in my whole life, I guess."

"I mean, he's Aaron Donald. People lose sleep from him. Obviously, I have the utmost respect for him. He's still going to be him. He's still going to be a game wrecker, somebody that can change the game."

Asked if he was losing sleep over facing Donald, Sisi said he wasn't.

"Nah," he said. "I usually go in with a neutral mentality. I adopted this when I was at Miami — nameless, faceless. It doesn't matter who you're facing. You've just got to trust your own technique and your own playing style."

That being said, Mauigoa feels he knows what to expect from Donald.

"He's going to be the type of guy that is going to do whatever he wants to do," Mauigoa said. "It can be a pain in the ass. But he made a name for himself with it — a person that doesn't have a tap-out button. He'll keep going and keep going."

articles.title: Florida State’s lack of depth underscores poor offseason personnel decisions
articles.summary: The last two games have shown the Seminoles’ ongoing roster building flaws.
articles.body:
Florida State finally looked like the team the coaching staff promised in the offseason.

Ashton Daniels and the offense moved the ball downfield at will as the Seminoles scored touchdowns on three of their first four drives. On defense, Tony White miraculously forced Alabama into three-and-outs on their first two drives. The Noles led 21-6 and had the Tide facing a third-and-17 with four minutes to go in the first half.

Then, the next 34 minutes of game action happened.

FSU's defense allowed points on nine straight drives as the personnel melted down and the coaching staff couldn't adjust. On offense, the Noles finished the game with explosive plays but poor game management, resulting in two touchdowns, two turnovers, and a lifeline for Alabama to get back in the contest at the end of the first half. Ultimately, the performance wasn't good enough, no matter how the game started.

The Seminoles had an extra week to prepare, while Alabama returned from an SEC road game. But once the Tide got their feet under them and made adjustments, they went on a 37-7 run, with no answers from the Florida State coaching staff.

"We have to be able to get off the field, and we showed the capability early in the game," a dejected Mike Norvell said after the game. "We allowed too many explosive plays tonight. … As their run game got going later in the game, it did wear on us.

"Not good enough when you give up over 550 yards of offense."

Of course, as with everything related to Florida State this season, you can't look at it in a vacuum. Poor offseason personnel decisions left the team lacking depth, especially on defense. The Seminoles held Alabama to 13 yards on 10 rushes in the first quarter and then allowed 124 yards on 14 carries in the fourth quarter.

No example better displayed the lack of bodies than Alabama's final touchdown drive of the game. FSU pulled within seven and backed the Crimson Tide up to their own 10-yard line thanks to a holding penalty. Kalen DeBoer's team proceeded to run the ball on eight of the next nine plays, including a 20-yard touchdown run, to close out the game. Once again, Florida State's defensive line lacked playmakers, with no sacks and only three tackles for loss from the front seven in yesterday's game, and was worn out by the end.

."It really has nothing to do with effort or want to," linebacker Chris Jones told the media postgame. "It has to do with execution. They came out with different things, and we did not execute the right way. … They came out with more of a gap scheme at the beginning of the game. Then, they started running more stretch and outside zone.

"We were in bad spots in a lot of those plays."

The big-money defensive acquisitions have not delivered for the Noles. The Seminoles brought in new coach Nick Williams to coach the edges and help ease the load on defensive line coach Terrance Knighton. Nobody on the defensive front seems to have taken a step forward this year. The Desir twins, who FSU paid to keep out of the transfer portal, are being asked to play more than they should because of the lack of depth and finished the game with a combined 0.5 tackles for loss and no sacks. Up the middle, Daniel Lyons has yet to take over a game the way the coaching staff hoped, and the players behind him, Kevin Wynn and Jordan Sanders, aren't providing enough to spell him. The defensive front did a good job containing Alabama quarterback Keelon Russell early in the game with rush-lane integrity, but his 57-yard touchdown run felt like the death blow in the third quarter.

"There was an element late where we definitely got worn down and being on the field," Norvell lamented. "There were a few times when we had a self-inflicted miss in alignment. There are big plays when no edge shows up.

"I thought we defended the run really well early, and it was unfortunate to see where it went to."

Even if it was more apparent on defense, Florida State's lack of offensive depth showed in the second half, too. After Norvell's well-designed early-game scripts, the Noles struggled to match that impact later. FSU's offensive line, which inserted Paul Bowling at right guard and kept Nate Pabst at right tackle, struggled to keep Ashton Daniels upright with a clean pocket to throw and create open rushing lanes.

Part of that also fell on Daniels, who struggled to process the field quickly, but the Seminoles still rushed for under four yards per carry (3.6) with sack yardage taken out. Norvell's offense moved the ball on big plays, as 344 of Daniels' 377 passing yards came on 10 plays, but the Seminoles lack the talent to push defenses back drive after drive.

"We had some missed opportunities on drives on offense that we have to have. You come on the road in a hostile environment against a good football team, you have to capitalize on those," Norvell said.

A little over a year ago, the Seminoles convincingly defeated Alabama and made 2024 feel like a blip. Yesterday, the Tide spotted Florida State 15 points and still won by two touchdowns. The program's decline is obvious, and poor evaluations and portal pickups are a major reason for it.

articles.title: 2026 Mountain West Football Week 3 Recap
articles.summary: Expected blowouts, standout performances, and a descent into the depths of Hell highlighted the MW slate in Week 3.
articles.body:
Week 3 of the 2026 season is in the books, and it was a lot milder for the Mountain West as a whole. The limited slate of games saw just two one-score contests, one of which saw a known contender assert themselves as a national threat, and the other seeing a hopeful contender sinking straight back into being an embarrassment to their fans. Without further ado, let's get into the MW slate in Week 3.

The Scoop: There is but one takeaway from a performance like this: Jay Sawvel is as good as gone in Laramie. Entering this game, Central Michigan had just narrowly beaten FCS team Colgate by scoring just 13 points, serving up the second worst offense in the country in terms of yardage. The Chips proceeded to have their best game of the season by far against the Cowboys, beating Wyoming by 14 in a game that was nowhere near as close as the final score would indicate.

Central Michigan had their way with Wyoming on the ground, carrying the ball 59 times for a whopping 339 yards and three touchdowns. QB Angel Flores, while completing just four passes for 32 yards, was still the engine of the offense, racking up 28 carries for 163 yards and two of those touchdowns. Flores' counterpart, Tyler Hughes, was absolutely abhorrent on the day, completing just 14 of 30 passes for 173 yards and two interceptions.

Wyoming was able to somewhat get the run game going, averaging 5.8 YPC on their 28 carries, but a sizeable portion of that production came after the Cowboys went down 24-3 at the end of the third quarter. To be precise, 193 of Wyoming's 342 total yards came in the fourth quarter, once the Chippewas were simply playing to close the game out. There is no way to spin this outcome that is not a complete embarrassment for Wyoming, which now looks like it will be one of the worst teams in the country this season.

Wyoming (1-2) will travel back home to Laramie for their conference opener next week, hosting the equally struggling Hawaii Rainbow Warriors (1-2, 0-1 MW) on Sept. 26 at 1:00 p.m. MDT. Hawaii was on a bye this week, but had finally gotten their season back on track somewhat with a win over New Mexico State the week before. This will be a battle of who wants to lose more, which by the looks of things will end up being the Cowboys. There will almost certainly be a coaching change before the end of the season here.

The Scoop: This game ended up being a tale of two halves. In the first half, UTEP took it to Michigan in the Big House, consistently exposing the Wolverines ' many flaws. The Miners capitalized on two Michigan fumbles to put themselves up 14-7 midway through the second quarter, sparking dreams of a miracle upset, shades of 2007 Appalachian State. Unfortunately, after that, the Miners had just 32 yards of offense the rest of the way, all while Michigan scored on every single remaining drive, save for kneeling out the end of the game. UTEP played admirably for a while, but once Michigan started taking the game somewhat seriously, there was very little the Miners could actually do.

UTEP (1-2) will travel back to El Paso for an important nonconference contest next week, hosting the Oregon State Beavers (1-2) on Sept. 26 at 7:00 p.m. MDT. Oregon State started their season off with two straight losses, albeit both competitive contests against top-25 teams. OSU is led by an explosive offense, highlighted by the nation's leading receiver, freshman Jesse Legree. UTEP likely won't keep this one very close, but it is an important contest nonetheless.

The Scoop: Turns out the Western Kentucky game was nothing more than an enormous fluke after all. Jeff Choke made his triumphant return, as the Wolf Pack blew a fourth-quarter lead with a cavalcade of bad play-calling and stupid mistakes, losing to Middle Tennessee by one score for the second year in a row. This game went the exact way I expected, the only difference was the fact that MTSU got one more field goal than I expected them to.

Carter Jones made his return from his dubious injury, accounting for 212 yards of offense, a rushing TD, and a terrible interception at the Blue Raiders' 11-yard line that killed a potential scoring drive in the third quarter. Nevada also fumbled twice inside their own 30-yard line, both of which led to Blue Raider touchdowns. In addition, the Pack had a Gerick Robinson punt return TD overturned due to an unnecessary holding penalty away from the ball. To be frank, however, Nevada would have never been in this game at all if not for several MTSU penalties, the vast majority of which were on third down.

Nevada averaged just 2.2 YPC on their 34 rush attempts, weighed down heavily by several disastrous jet sweeps, as well as a 4th and 2 run up the gut in the fourth quarter that sealed Nevada's long-obvious fate. Even without those terrible plays, the Wolf Pack would have still wound up stifled by MTSU's defense, which racked up four TFLs and a sack-fumble on Jones. I haven't even mentioned Nevada's defense being destroyed by MTSU's backfield, which racked up 157 rushing yards and just one play for negative yards all night long.

Nevada is now a disgusting 3-10 in one-score games in the last three seasons. This was simply a performance going back to classic Nevada under Jeff Choate, whose seat would be flaming-hot if not for the fact that the university already has a massive buyout to pay out due to their last failure of a head coaching hire. Just another day in Reno, I guess.

Nevada (1-2) will travel back to Northern Nevada to host Air Force (1-1, 0-1 MW) for their conference opener on Sept. 26 at 7:30 p.m. PDT. The Pack have not beaten the Falcons since 2018, and Air Force was blown out by North Dakota State in their conference opener, but given Coach Choate's previous comments about revenge games, Nevada will be playing with zero extra passion, execution, or urgency in this contest. Air Force has shown typically excellent ability to run the ball with their triple-option offense, which does not bode well for Nevada, given how they were ripped apart on the ground last night. No matter what, this game will result in yet another one-score loss

The Scoop: I predicted New Mexico would keep it very close with Oklahoma in this one, and they did exactly that. On a night dominated by defense, the Lobos trailed just 7-6 at halftime, forcing John Mateer into mistake after mistake while completely shutting down OU's run game. Unfortunately, UNM's offense never got going in this one, going scoreless in the second half to walk away with a hard-fought, yet ultimately disappointing 14-6 loss. The Lobos' defense is going to be a problem this season, and they deserve a medal for how they shut down the Sooners' offense in this game. They forced four puntes, three turnovers, a sack, and six TFLs on the night, keeping the OU offense in check all night.

New Mexico's biggest problem was their cycle of quarterback hokey-pokey continuing in this match, as Teo Fa'avae and Luke Moga each completed four passes for a combined 116 yards and no touchdowns or interceptions. This allowed OU's defense to focus on the run, averaging just 1.6 YPC on the Lobos' 38 attempts. One of New Mexico's offensive lapses was particularly painful, as the Lobos got the ball at Oklahoma's 39-yard line after a muffed punt, only to go three-and-out with -1 yards on the drive. Get something on that drive and maybe UNM's game-ending turnover on downs looks a little bit different. Nonetheless, the Lobos have arrived in the national spotlight. They are frontrunners for the CFP in 2026, especially if they can get their offense sorted out.

New Mexico (2-1) will travel back to the Land of Enchantment next weekend, only they won't be going to Albuquerque. Instead, they will be heading down south to take on loathed in-state rivals New Mexico State (1-2) on Sept. 26 at 1:30 p.m. MDT. NMSU was on a bye this week, with their previous game being a 10-point loss at Hawaii. The Aggies should be no threat to the Lobos given the latter's level of performance this season, but that doesn't mean that they will be shown any mercy in this contest.

The Scoop: I'll give the Huskies some credit here, they played much better than I expected they would. NIU was clearly playing mad early in this one, jumping out to a 10-0 lead while outgaining the Wildcats 106 to minus-five. After that, the Wildcats went on a 42-0 run that involved QB Noah Fifita breaking Arizona's all-time passing record, going 31-of-34 for 325 yards with four TDs and no INTs. In his first start as a Huskie, Taron Dickens completed 25 passes for 228 yards and a TD with no turnovers, so there is certainly potential offensively. I will need to see more from the Huskies' defense to truly believe in their ability to win in the Mountain West, but games like this where they actually show some life give me far more hope than their blowout loss to Iowa. Good game, NIU. You're getting there.

NIU (0-3) will complete their nonconference schedule with a trip to Atlanta, GA to take on the Georgia State Panthers (2-1) on Sept. 26 at 1:00 p.m. CDT. Whereas the Panthers would normally be a total pushover, they are off to a hot start this season, taking down reigning C-USA champion Kennesaw State on the road and giving UCF more than their fair share this weekend. This would be a big win for the Huskies if they can pull it off.

The Scoop: A great bounceback win here for UTEP, who took their frustrations out on poor Texas Southern, destroying them for the game's last 35 minutes. After the Tigers took the lead, 10-7 in the second quarter, the Miners scored the game's final 44 points for a convincing win via rout. E.J. Colson threw for 239 yards and four touchdowns, while the Miners' 33 carries resulted in 252 yards and three touchdowns. Tiger QBs were held to just 99 passing yards and an interception, and Texas Southern's offense was held to just 34 yards after taking their 10-7 lead. This was a typical FCS win, but an impressive one for the Miners nonetheless.

UTEP (1-1) will travel next week to Ann Arbor, MI to take on the Michigan Wolverines at 1:30 p.m. MDT on Big Ten Network. Michigan's official record is 2-0, but the college football world, AP voters, and basic logic and reason state that they lost their home opener to Western Michigan before taking down a struggling Oklahoma the next week. UTEP already was blown out by the Sooners, so playing the Wolverines will likely not bring better results to the fans in El Paso.

The Scoop: One may look at the 21-point margin of victory here and say that Sac State performed better against the Bison than expected, but I'd say this has more to do with NDSU offensive sluggishness in the second half than anything the Hornets pulled on the field. Nathan Hayes completed just 14 of 24 passes, and the Bison only had 362 yards of offense, but one must also consider the fact that the Bison led 28-0 with 11:24 left in the second quarter and ask whether NDSU was even trying after that. This was a thorough beatdown, but NDSU never pulled their starters so I supposed the Hornets have earned a slight pat on the back for that. The Bison, meanwhile, look just as imposing a threat to the Mountain West as they have all season. The CFP is a real possibility now.

North Dakota State finally has their first bye week of the season this week, returning when they host their first home conference game against Wyoming (1-2) on Oct. 3 at 2:30 p.m. CDT. Wyoming is a terrible team on the verge of firing their coach, so I have no problem believing that this will be an utter rout with the Bison having a full week to prepare.

The Scoop: Finally, we have the game that you can't help but wish had been better than it was. The first 50 minutes of this game were a defensive showcase, with neither team's quarterback ever looking comfortable. The Bulldogs led 6-3 at the half, and the game was 13-10 after a SJSU touchdown in the fourth quarter. After that, however, the Spartans had two interceptions and two turnovers on downs on their last four drives, making the final score look far worse than it actually was.

The two teams were evenly matched in nearly every statistical category, save for turnovers, where the Spartans lost the battle (and the game) 4-0. Luke Weaver threw for 244 yards and a TD, but had a dreadful four interceptions against a 'Dogs defense that had just one on the season prior to this game. Worse yet, three of the four picks were on deep balls thrown inside Fresno State's 40-yard line, killing all momentum SJSU had at the worst possible times. Probably the more alarming stat was Jabari Bates going for just 94 yards on 19 carries, showcasing the main way the Bulldogs found to beat the Spartans: you beat Bates, you beat San Jose State. At least Anthony Ivey (7-for-150) starred at wideout, but that's about as comforting as a blanket made out of a cactus at this point. This was nothing short of total deflation for San Jose State, which is a bad thing to happen at the outset of conference play.

San Jose State (2-2) will have their first bye week of the season this week, preparing for a trip to Honolulu to face Hawaii (1-2, 0-1 MW) on Oct. 3 at 9:00 p.m. PDT. Hawaii has had their fair share of struggles as of late, so perhaps a trip for Luke Weaver to face the freshman that beat him out for the starting job a year ago will motivate this team to come out swinging. Hopefully for Spartan fans' sakes, those swings don't lead to a high turnover count this time.

articles.title: Michigan Football freshman edge rusher Tariq Boney impresses vs UTEP
articles.summary: While he didn’t see the field much in the first two games, Tariq Boney made his presence felt for Michigan Football in Week 3:
articles.body:
The college football world has officially been introduced to Tariq Boney. Michigan's freshman edge rusher had only one snap in the first two weeks of the season, but ended Week 3 against UTEP with four total tackles, including 1.5 TFLs and one sack.

Before his formal introduction to the college football world, Boney's name circulated around the media, as he was often mentioned by head coach Kyle Whittingham and defensive coordinator Jay Hill for having a great fall camp.

On multiple occasions leading up to the first game, Whittingham and Hill praised Boney, as well as his freshman edge rushing counterpart Carter Meadows who has been dealing with injuries and made his first career appearance against UTEP.

On August 21, Whittingham said "Two freshman defensive ends, Carter Meadows and Tariq Boney, are having an outstanding camp, and they're gonna be involved."

Hill on August 26 said "Tariq Boney and Carter Meadows have done unbelievable things for freshmen," and emphasized a similar sentiment on September 2, saying "as a young freshman, has really done some great things."

In Boney's lone snap against the Sooners, he came off the right side and bulldozed past the offensive lineman. Boney's rush forced quarterback John Mateer to step up in the pocket to avoid the pressure and escape a sack.

UTEP quarterback EJ Colson Jr. didn't have the same luck against Boney.

Near the end of the third quarter, Boney lined up in the same spot he did in the play against Oklahoma. He bulldozed past the offensive lineman yet again, avoided the pick-up block from the running back and sacked Colson.

"His quickness, his explosion, he is a powerful guy," Whittingham said after Michigan took down UTEP 52-17. "He's built like a fire hydrant and strong as an ox in the weight room. Just his strength and explosion is as good as I've ever seen in a true freshman. … He's got a very developed body and relentless motor. His motor never shuts down. He's constantly in pursuit."

Boney proved his ability to produce constant pursuit, coming up with 1.5 TFLs in addition to his first-career sack. Boney was in a group of 12 Wolverines who recorded at least 0.5 TFLs on the day, and Boney tied for the lead on the team with 1.5 TFLs alongside sophomore Benny Patterson III.

This type of performance, despite being his first significant playing time on a Saturday, was not unexpected from his teammates.

"It's definitely in line with what I've seen in practice," sophomore Chase Taylor said. "He played for sure because you can see that he's got the size, talent, build, speed. It's just coming together."

As a true freshman, Boney is starting to make a name for himself with a stellar performance against the Miners. And if Saturday was any indication, it's going to be hard to keep Boney off the field in the coming weeks.

articles.title: Three takeaways from UNC’s wildly frustrating loss to Clemson
articles.summary: The Heels now have some big issue to sort out during the bye week.
articles.body:
I'm not even sure where to begin. When Clemson punted with 7:06 left in the 2nd quarter, Carolina ran it back to the Clemson 46 while holding a 17-3 lead. A 14-point lead, with the ball in field position that often results in points, had UNC fans feeling confident. To that point in the game and season, Clemson's offense was 4-33 on third downs and had scored one touchdown. UNC already had 195 yards of offense, including 112 on the ground. The game seemed headed towards a UNC romp.

From that point forward, Clemson would outscore UNC 25-3 and outgain the Tar Heels by 218 yards. Clemson's comeback started slowly, gathered momentum, and then ended emphatically after a three hour weather delay.

Billy Edwards may have lost his job as UNC's starting quarterback

You can blame me for Edwards' meltdown. Midway through the second quarter, I contributed to the staff chat this observation: "Won't be this game, but Billy Edwards' inability to to hit downfield is going to be a problem." To that point, Edwards had misfired on several downfield attempts to Shipp and Thurman, but the efficiency coming from the run game and short passing game had the offense moving the ball.

Edwards' accuracy with longer throws was a concern coming into the game. Against TCU and ETSU, Edwards was 21-23 on throws travelling less than 10 yards downfield but only 10-24 on throws deeper than that. After the first quarter, Clemson adjusted, compressing their coverage and putting more pressure on the pocket. Their goal was clear — make Billy Edwards beat them with his arm on longer throws. And he couldn't.

From the point in the first half that UNC had the ball at the Clemson 46 up 17-3, Edwards stat line was 7-16 for 56 yards and an interception. Edwards for the day finished 13-30 for 152 yards with a touchdown and an interception. Against this same Clemson defense, LSU threw for 334 yards, and Georgia Southern's Max Johnson — yes, that Max Johnson — threw for 244. Edwards' inability over three games to connect downfield consistently, with weapons like Jelani Thurman and Jordan Shipp at his disposal, was a fatal flaw against Clemson, one likely to be just as fatal against the rest of ACC competition.

Bill Belichick has a lot of thinking to do about his quarterback position. The question isn't whether or not Edwards can elevate his game. It's whether UNC has anyone in the QB room capable of performing better.

Clemson's fast pace exposed UNC's defensive depth and communication

UNC was down Melkart Abou Jaoude for this game. One aspect of depth is having a "next man up" at key positions. For MAJ, that's Donovan Hoilette, who transferred from FCS Richmond. Hoilette finished the day with two tackles, and Clemson found some success working his edge in the run game. Hoilette contributed no sacks or QB pressures. Missing MAJ hurt.

The other aspect of depth is dealing with teams that will try to run pace, and Clemson enjoyed a lot of success when trying to move fast against Belichick's defense. Clemson worked with pace on its final first half drive that ended with a field goal and sent the game into halftime down 17-6. The drive took over five minutes, but Clemson ran 18 plays and moved the ball 88 yards, going 3-4 on third downs. Clemson's true freshman QB, Tait Reynolds, looked much more comfortable operating in that mode. Clemson kept it up in the 2nd half, averaging 7.3 yards per rush and 13.9 per pass attempt.

Initially, it appeared that physical fatigue might be the most significant issue with the pace, as UNC's defense seemed gassed by the time weather put a halt to the game midway through the fourth quarter. However, after that three hour delay, Clemson's first possession went 68 yards in four plays. It appears that moving quickly short-circuited defensive communication, both between the sidelines and the defensive captain as well as among the players on the field.

Expect to see more of this from opponents until UNC figures out the communication and substitution issues exposed by Clemson's pace of play.

In two P4 games now, Bobby Petrino's offense disappears after the first quarter

UNC against TCU and Clemson scored 24 points in the opening frame. In the succeeding six quarters of play, UNC's offense has managed all of nine points. In the first quarter against TCU, UNC averaged 7.42 yards per play on 19 plays. Against Clemson in the first, UNC averaged 6.7 yards per play on 19 plays. In the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th quarters of those two games, UNC has averaged 4.56 yards per play. UNC's 2-11 on third down conversions in the second half of those games. Any way you cut it, the offense starts hot and then somehow turns into last year's offense.

The play-calling, long considered Petrino's wheelhouse, was odd at times in this game as well. For the moment, we'll begin and end with the 4th and one play late that sealed UNC's fate. Edwards' struggles with accuracy the further downfield the play design were noted above. UNC needed a yard to sustain a drive that had to end in points. Petrino called for a play action shot deep downfield to Jelani Thurman, a play which didn't fool Clemson and a pass from Edwards that gave Thurman no chance at making a catch or drawing a flag.

With only a two game sample to work with, the overly simple explanation appears to be that Petrino's initial game plan works spectacularly well. Then, opponents adjust, and UNC has no answers to the adjustments. The QB issues noted above contribute to that, but unless Belichick is forcing his hand, Petrino's chosen the QB he feels represents UNC's best chance to win games.

Bill Belichick's team collapsed against Clemson . The remote chance remains that Clemson rips through much of its remaining schedule in the same way it ripped through UNC after finding its footing late in the first half. However, Clemson's success came through superior scheme and execution, not overwhelming talent. The Tar Heels' future opponents were taking notes. With a bye week to prepare for Notre Dame, Belichick has two weeks to figure out how to not let that game be completely embarrassing. Then, Belichick has get back on the winning side of football games in UNC's final eight. If he doesn't, those will be the final eight games of Belichick's coaching career.

articles.title: 2 Cowboys to buy, 2 to sell versus the Commanders
articles.body:
Week 2 is here, and the Dallas Cowboys are looking for a bounce-back week after a tough loss to the New York football Giants . Let's look at some players to buy/sell for Week 2.

Pickens almost feels like a given. He had some massive drops against the Giants; one might have been a touchdown. As is often the criticism of Pickens, his focus and intensity might not always be at 100%. His Week 1 stat line is marginal. Three catches for 28 yards on six targets. He drew more penalty yardage than actual receiving yards, racking up 38 total yards on Giants penalties. So even on an off night, he still made an impact.

What's more, Pickens led the Cowboys with a 16.1-yard average depth of target and 37.9% of the team's air yards, signaling the kind of role the Cowboys see for him.

Washington offers a logical bounce-back opportunity. The Commanders' secondary is already dealing with the absence of Trey Amos , while Washington cornerback Mike Sainristil was criticized heavily for a poor Week 1 performance. Saying Pickens is "due" for a bounce-back seems cliché, but Week 2 could very well be that moment for the 2025 Pro Bowler.

Ferguson had a tough game in Week 1. He only had six yards on two catches while being targeted six times against the G-Men. Dallas views the TE position like they do their running backs. A well-rounded player who can block and make plays. With Washington bringing an aggressive defensive scheme, Dallas can't afford to have its tight end become a liability when he's attached to the formation.

Then you have to consider the rise of Brevyn Spann-Ford and the many receivers that Dak Prescott has at his disposal. Ferguson's impact seems capped at occasional catches, and without some of the flash he could have shown, there may not be enough room for him to have a huge impact. Even still, the Commanders just gave up a huge game to Dallas Goedert , so anything could happen.

Ezeiruaku was arguably the Cowboys' best defender in Week 1. Yes, he had moments when he lost discipline on the edge and struggled in coverage, but he finished with 10 tackles, a half-sack, a tackle for loss and two pressures, and Dallas' official site notes that he earned the team's highest PFF grade at 86.5.

Now look at the matchup. Washington's starting left tackle is Brandon Coleman , filling in for injured Laremy Tunsil . Coleman allowed seven pressures and a sack against Philadelphia , while Washington's starting tackles allowed 15 pressures combined.

On top of that, Commanders QB Jayden Daniels tends to hold onto the ball too long. Daniels took a league-leading 3.41 seconds to throw in Week 1. That's a gift to a pass rush that desperately needs to get home. Ezeiruaku showed in Week 1 that he can create disruption. Week 2 gives him an opportunity to turn that disruption into production.

There are so many questions surrounding this group, and now that Overshown is out, even more doubt can creep into that position group. Dallas gave up 165 rushing yards to the Giants in Week 1, and the defense allowed New York to convert 82% of its third downs. The linebacking group was part of a larger defensive problem: Dallas struggled to consistently fit the run and communicate in coverage.

Now rookie third-round pick Jaishawn Barham will take over at MIKE and wear the green dot in his second NFL game. Head coach Brian Schottenheimer said Barham has "great command" of the defense, but that's still a significant responsibility for a rookie.

The problem is that Washington presents a similar challenge to Jaxson Dart and the Giants. Jayden Daniels is a mobile quarterback. Washington also ran for 132 yards against Philadelphia, with Jacory Croskey-Merritt carrying 16 times for 63 yards and Daniels adding 31 yards. That means Dallas' linebackers will have to diagnose quickly while also accounting for the quarterback as a runner.

And that's before you factor in the loss of Overshown, who normally relays Christian Parker's calls to the defense. Parker said this week that he trusts Barham, Dee Winters and Shemar James to step into the role, but the Cowboys will clearly be asking more of that trio than they expected entering the season.

Can Dallas' linebackers clean up their Week 1 mistakes while also replacing the guy who was supposed to run the defense? A significant ask at this point.

articles.title: Explosive! Cowboys paths to Week 2 victory revealed
articles.summary: If the Cowboys want to beat the Commanders, they need better special teams play, better third-down defense, and more explosive plays on offense.
articles.body:
The Dallas Cowboys and Washington Commanders are both 0-1, coming off division losses. Each team will be desperate to avoid falling into a 0-2 NFC East hole, especially the Cowboys as they are at home. The Commanders have a mobile quarterback in Jayden Daniels , similar to Jaxson Dart . Otherwise, they aren't comparable to the New York Giants roster, so the issues New York created for the Dallas defense won't be the same.

The Dallas defense was the main issue in Week 1. Whether it was a matchup problem or they're just a bad unit, but a win for the Cowboys in Week 2 will be more about all three phases than the defense. The offense has to be better facing a poor defensive opponent and the special teams must resolve their field-position issues. Here are the keys to a Dallas victory over the Commanders.

The lack of explosive plays against the Giants might have been the biggest shock from that contest . An explosive play is a 10-yard rush or a 20-yard pass. With options like CeeDee Lamb , George Pickens , and Ryan Flournoy for Dak Prescott to throw to, explosive passes should be regular for them, but they didn't have a single reception for 20 yards.

The rushing attack had minimal explosive plays last season, so not having many isn't surprising, but the running backs had zero. The only explosive play for the Cowboys in Week 1 was a 10-yard scramble by Prescott. Dallas has to attack the Washington defense with a downfield passing attack, and hopefully explosive runs can develop as they wear down the Washington defense.

The Cowboys' offense had the second-best third-down conversion rate of opening week, but the problem is the only team ahead of them was their opponent, the Giants. New York was 9-for-10 on third-down conversions before a kneel-down on a third down at the end of the game. They weren't thought of as a juggernaut, but the Cowboys defense made them look like one.

The Giants converted four plays of third-and-9 or longer, and the only unsuccessful play of that kind was the kneel-down to end the game. This is as obvious as it can get for any team, for any week, but if Dallas allows anywhere close to the same success rate on third down to the Commanders, they'll end the game 0-2.

Last season, the Cowboys had the worst starting field position of any team in the NFL, and the issue continued in game one of 2026. Dallas kick returns went for 25, 17, 31, 24, and 25, for an average of 24 yards per return. They also had a penalty on the second return of the game. The punter had a good game, averaging nearly 50 yards per punt, and both punts landed inside the 20. Brandon Aubrey missed one of his three extra points.

The kickers are both All-Pro players and should continue to perform well, but the return game falloff is a significant problem. KaVontae Turpin is a multiple-time All-Pro, but since John Fassel left and Nick Sorensen took the job, the return game has been awful. Putting the offense behind in the field position battle has to be limited. The Cowboys defense and special teams set up their offense to require perfection, and that isn't possible for 17 games a year.

You can find Mike Crum on Twitter @cdpiglet or on YouTube at Across the Cowboys podcast

articles.title: See Titans RB Julius Chestnut wearing Halloween costume before Eagles game
articles.summary: See Tennessee Titans running back Julius Chestnut's Halloween costume entrance before kickoff vs. the Philadelphia Eagles.
articles.body:
The Tennessee Titans might log their hottest home game in franchise history against the Philadelphia Eagles on Sept. 20 (noon, FOX).

Heat indexes could reach the triple-digits, so fall is not in the air.

But that didn't stop Titans running back and special-teamer Julius Chestnut from looking toward Halloween — again. He arrived at Nissan Stadium wearing a Marvel Green Goblin costume, one week after wearing a Black Panther costume to the season opener.
